vignette:
Kiran traces the faint, silvery scar on their left wrist, a permanent reminder etched into their skin. It’s an unconscious habit, something their fingers find while they stare at the lines of code on their monitor, trying to locate a bug in the system. The logic of the code used to be a sanctuary, a predictable world of if-then statements and clean execution. Now, it’s just another screen where the ghosts appear.

Before the protest eighteen months ago, Kiran’s life was built on that kind of logic. As a senior software engineer, they managed a team, built complex systems, and found a deep satisfaction in creating order from digital chaos. They and their wife, Meera, had a comfortable life in their quiet suburban home. They were politically engaged but not front-line activists. The rally downtown was the first they had attended in years, a solidarity march for immigrant rights. Kiran remembers the feeling of the crowd—hopeful, vibrant, a sea of families and handmade signs.

The shift was sudden, a change in atmospheric pressure. The chanting faltered as the first line of police in riot gear appeared at the end of the street. Kiran remembers the sun glinting off their helmets, turning them into an anonymous, menacing wall. The memory isn’t a linear story anymore; it’s a collection of sensory fragments that crash into their consciousness without warning. The percussive thud of a canister hitting the pavement. The acrid bite of tear gas catching in their throat. The panicked surge of the crowd, a wave that knocked them off their feet.

The most vivid fragment is the weight. The crushing pressure of a knee in their back, pinning them to the hot asphalt. The rough scrape of the pavement against their cheek. The world became a blur of black boots and yelling. They remember trying to explain they weren't resisting, but the words were lost. The plastic rasp of zip-ties pulled brutally tight around their wrists was the last sound they focused on before being hauled to their feet. The ride in the van, the hours in a crowded holding cell, the dismissive paperwork—it all felt profoundly dehumanizing, as if their identity had been stripped away and replaced with a case number.

Meera found them hours later, looking small and pale under the fluorescent lights of the precinct. The drive home was silent. Kiran couldn't find the words to explain the shame and terror that had taken root in their bones.

Now, that terror dictates the terms of their life. They work almost exclusively from home, using the pandemic as a convenient excuse to avoid the office, the commute, the city. The truth is, the thought of going downtown makes their heart hammer against their ribs. Sirens in the distance are no longer background noise; they are a direct threat, sending a jolt of adrenaline through their body that leaves them trembling. They’ve abandoned their evening walks with Meera. Last month, they were in a grocery store when a security guard raised his voice at a teenager, and Kiran had to flee, leaving a full cart in the aisle as they gasped for air in the parking lot.

Sleep offers little respite. They often wake up tangled in their sheets, the feeling of pressure on their back so real they can’t breathe. During the day, they are perpetually on edge, irritable over the smallest things—a dish left in the sink, a meeting running five minutes late. They see the worry in Meera’s eyes but feel separated from her by a wall of glass. She reaches for them, and they flinch.

They sit at their desk, the bug in the code still unfound. An image flashes—the glint of sunlight on a helmet—and the lines on the screen swim out of focus. Their own mind feels like faulty code, stuck in an infinite loop, replaying a trauma they can’t debug. They close their eyes, tracing the scar on their wrist, and wait for the feeling to pass.
